content_voiceover: Virchow's triad is the classic conceptual framework for understanding why thrombosis occurs, and it's foundational for boards. The three components are stasis, meaning sluggish or stagnant blood flow that allows clotting factors and platelets to accumulate locally instead of being washed away, vascular endothelial injury, damage to the vessel wall that exposes tissue factor and subendothelial collagen, triggering both the coagulation cascade and platelet activation, and hypercoagulability, an intrinsic or acquired shift in the blood's balance toward clot formation, whether from inherited thrombophilia, malignancy, pregnancy, or other acquired states. Virtually every clinical scenario of venous or arterial thrombosis you'll encounter on boards can be mapped back to one or more of these three mechanisms, so it's worth having this framework ready as your first mental checklist whenever a thrombosis case comes up.
keypoints: Stasis, sluggish blood flow allowing local accumulation of clotting factors
Vascular endothelial injury, exposes tissue factor and triggers cascade
Hypercoagulability, intrinsic or acquired shift favoring clot formation
Framework applies to nearly all venous and arterial thrombosis cases
keypoint_voiceover: Keep Virchow's triad as your go to framework, stasis, vascular endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Any thrombosis case you see on boards will map back to at least one of these three mechanisms.
